2.content: The event loop, the goroutine pool, topic fan-out and batched dispatch behind a varmq worker, with interactive scenes.

7.content: What batching means for your code

8.content: Each worker has two moving parts: one **event loop** that decides what runs next, and a **pool** of goroutines that run your function. A job travels from `Add`, through the queue and the event loop, to a pool goroutine. The scenes below are models of the library. Each one steps through a single case, and you can step through it yourself.

9.content: Every worker runs one event loop, a single goroutine. It sleeps until something signals it: `Add` putting a job in the queue, or a pool goroutine finishing work. On each signal it hands jobs to the pool while the queue has work and a slot is free, then goes back to sleep.

10.content: A slot is free while the number of busy pool goroutines is below the worker's concurrency. If no slot is free, the loop waits for a goroutine to come back.

11.content: Every `Add`, and every job in an `AddAll`, tries to wake the event loop. The signal channel holds only one pending signal, so the extra signals are dropped. That is enough: one wake-up lets the loop keep dispatching back to back while the queue has work and a slot is free. A signal that arrives while another is pending costs nothing.

12.content: The concurrency limit is an upper bound, not a pool size. The pool starts with one idle goroutine and spawns more while another one would drain the backlog faster than it costs. When a goroutine finishes, it stays in the pool if more jobs are waiting than idle goroutines are ready to run them. Otherwise it exits, and the pool shrinks back to one idle goroutine. The scenes label the goroutines Worker 1, Worker 2 and so on. `WithIdleWorkerExpiryDuration` and `WithMinIdleWorkerRatio` change how many idle goroutines stay around. Concurrency covers both.

13.content: Below, six jobs are added to a worker with concurrency 4. Four go out back to back, the other two wait in the queue, and the pool shrinks as it drains.

14.content: A `Topic` feeds the same event loop as a queue, but from a shared log instead of a queue of jobs. `Publish` appends the payload to the log once, then signals the event loop of every subscribed worker, the same one-slot signal `Add` sends. Each subscription reads the log through its own cursor, so each worker's loop makes its own job from the payload and hands it to its own pool. The workers run independently: a slow or paused one does not hold up `Publish` or the others.

15.content: A payload stays in the log until every subscription has read it.

16.content: Topics covers subscribing, capacity and priority.

17.content: A hand-off costs the event loop the same whether a job takes a nanosecond or a minute. With many short jobs, the loop, not the goroutines, becomes the bottleneck. To avoid that, a goroutine can take several jobs at once, a batch, and run them one after another.

18.content: The batch size is the smallest of three numbers:

19.content: an even split of the waiting jobs across the workers the limit allows;

20.content: enough jobs to keep hand-offs about 32 microseconds apart, sized from the last batch that finished (one job until a job has been timed, unless concurrency is 1);

21.content: With enough jobs waiting, that works out like this:

| ----------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| 10 goroutines, 3 s jobs | 1, so jobs start in queue order |

| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Concurrency 1, any jobs | up to 32, because one goroutine runs jobs in order anyway |

The first goroutine takes 4 jobs, a second goroutine is spawned for 2, and the last 2 jobs go out one at a time as goroutines free up. A fresh worker hands out one job at a time until its first batch finishes. Pick a row of the table, or set your own numbers, to see the batch size.

28.content: **Jobs waiting in a batch are still `Queued`.** The worker's `NumPending` counts them and `NumProcessing` does not. You can still close them.

29.content: **On `Stop` or `Pause`,** each goroutine finishes its running job and parks the rest of its batch. `NumPending` counts the parked jobs, but the queue's `Len()` does not. They run first, in order, after `Resume` or `Restart`, and `Purge` closes them. See the lifecycle.

30.content: **Capacity counts only jobs still in the queue.** A bounded queue can have up to 32 more jobs per goroutine pending, held in batches.

37.content: What a job is, the handle Add returns, job IDs and statuses, closing a queued job, and waiting on a job.

43.content: A job is one unit of work: your data, an optional ID, and a status that changes as the worker deals with it. You never build one yourself. `Add` creates it, puts it in the queue and, on an in-memory queue, hands you a handle.

44.content: The worker function and the code that called `Add` see different things.

45.content: **The worker function gets a `Job[T]`.** It has two methods: `Data()` returns what you passed to `Add`, and `ID()` returns the job's ID. The interface has nothing else: no status and no `Close`.

46.content: **The caller gets a handle.** `Add` returns the handle and a `bool`:

47.content: `ok` is `false` when the queue did not take the job: it is full or closed, or a job with the same ID is still in the queue (a job a worker has already taken into a batch, or parked, has released its ID). In that case `job` is `nil`, so check `ok` before you use it.

48.content: With a plain worker the handle is an `EnqueuedJob`. The other two worker types add one method that returns the outcome:

52.content: Every handle has `ID()`, `Status()`, `IsClosed()`, `Wait()` and `Close()`. `Err` and `Result` block until the job is closed, then return what the worker function sent. For a job that was closed before it ran, `Err` returns `nil` and `Result` returns the zero value and a `nil` error. See worker types for the three workers side by side.

53.content: A job has no ID unless you give it one. `ID()` returns an empty string by default.

54.content: `WithJobId` sets the ID of one job: `queue.Add(data, varmq.WithJobId("job-1"))`. An empty string is ignored.

55.content: `WithJobIdGenerator` sets a function that makes IDs. `Add` calls it, on the caller's goroutine, for every job; its value is used when the job has no ID of its own.

56.content: An in-memory queue refuses a second `Add` with an ID that a job still in the queue holds: it returns `ok == false`. A job a worker has already taken into a batch, or parked, has released its ID, so a duplicate `Add` is accepted even though that job's status still reads `Queued`. IDs from a generator are not checked. Items added with `AddAll` get a `g:` prefix, so an item with ID `a` shows up in the worker function as `g:a`. Job IDs covers the details.

57.content: `Status()` on a handle returns one of five strings:

58.content:
| Status    | Meaning                                                                                        |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Created` | The job exists but `Add` has not stored it yet. A handle you get back from `Add` is past this. |

59.content:
| Status   | Meaning                                                                                                                 |
| -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Queued` | The job is waiting. It may be in the queue, in a batch a worker took but has not started, or parked by a pause or stop. |

60.content:
| Status       | Meaning                            |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------- |
| `Processing` | The worker function is running it. |

61.content:
| Status     | Meaning                       |
| ---------- | ----------------------------- |
| `Finished` | The worker function returned. |

62.content:
| Status   | Meaning                                                         |
| -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Closed` | The job is done with: it ran, or it was closed before it could. |

63.content: `Finished` is short-lived. As soon as your function returns, the worker closes the job to release anyone waiting on it. By the time `Wait` returns, the status is `Closed`, and `IsClosed()` is `true`. So `Closed` does not tell you whether the job ran. Record that in your own worker function if it matters.

64.content: Move one job through its statuses below. Pick the worker type to see what the handle returns, and try `Close()` at each status.

65.content: The worker below runs one job at a time, and each job takes 500 ms. The program reads both statuses while job-1 runs.

66.content: job-1 is `Processing` and job-2 is `Queued`. After `Wait`, both read `Closed` and `IsClosed()` is `true`, though both ran.

67.content: `Close()` cancels a job that has not started. It only marks the job closed; it does not take it out of the queue. When the worker reaches a closed job it skips it, and your function never sees it. Closing also releases `Wait` at once.

68.content: It succeeds while the job waits. It fails in two cases:

69.content: A running job returns `ErrJobProcessing`. You cannot stop it from the outside.

70.content: A closed job returns `ErrJobAlreadyClosed`. That includes a job that already ran, since the worker closes those too.

71.content: Until the worker reaches it, a job closed while it waited still counts in the queue's `Len()` and in the worker's `NumPending()`. It counts as submitted, and because it never ran, it never counts as completed.

72.content: Here job-1 is running and job-2 and job-3 wait behind it.

73.content: Closing job-1 fails with `ErrJobProcessing`. Closing job-2 works, its `Wait` returns at once while job-1 is still running, and a second `Close` fails with `ErrJobAlreadyClosed`. The worker then runs job-3 and never prints a line for job-2.

74.content: `Wait()` blocks until the job is closed, whether it ran or you closed it. If that has already happened, it returns at once. To wait for everything a worker has queued instead of one job, see waiting.

76.content: The seven worker states, how Start, Pause, Resume, Stop and Restart move between them, and the settings WithAutoRun and WithStoppedRetention.

93.content: `Idle` and `Running` swap on their own as jobs start and finish, so `Running` is a moment, not a mode you set. `IsActive` is true for either of them, which makes it the check for "started and not paused or stopped".

95.content: The worker is `Initiated` until `Start`. `Start` makes it `Idle`, and it is `Running` a moment later, because jobs were already waiting. `Pause` returns while job 1 still runs, so the worker is `Pausing`. Once job 1 is done it is `Paused`, and jobs 2 and 3 wait until `Resume`. When they are done the worker is `Idle` again.

96.content: A status is a snapshot. Between reading it and acting on it the worker may have moved on. To know where a worker has landed after `Pause` or `Stop`, use the waiting helpers below.

97.content:
| Call    | From                   | Result | Errors from other states                                                                                  |
| ------- | ---------------------- | ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Start` | `Initiated`, `Stopped` | `Idle` | `ErrRunningWorker` from `Idle` or `Running`; `ErrWorkerPausing`, `ErrWorkerPaused` or `ErrWorkerStopping` |

| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Pause` | `Idle` becomes `Paused`; `Running` becomes `Pausing`, then `Paused` | already `Pausing` or `Paused`: no error | `ErrNotRunningWorker` from `Initiated`; `ErrWorkerStopping`; `ErrWorkerStopped` |

99.content:
| Call     | From                                                     | Result                                | Errors from other states                                                                            |
| -------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Resume` | `Paused` becomes `Idle`, and the worker pulls jobs again | already `Idle` or `Running`: no error | `ErrNotRunningWorker` from `Initiated`; `ErrWorkerPausing`; `ErrWorkerStopping`; `ErrWorkerStopped` |

100.content:
| Call   | From                                                                       | Result                                    | Errors from other states               |
| ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `Stop` | `Idle`, `Running`, `Pausing` or `Paused` become `Stopping`, then `Stopped` | already `Stopping` or `Stopped`: no error | `ErrNotRunningWorker` from `Initiated` |

101.content:
| Call      | From                      | Result                                           | Errors from other states               |
| --------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| `Restart` | any state but `Initiated` | stops, waits for `Stopped`, starts again: `Idle` | `ErrNotRunningWorker` from `Initiated` |

102.content: The errors are values in the package, listed under Variables. Two details:

103.content: `Pause`, `Resume` and `Stop` return at once. `Restart` does not: it waits for running jobs to finish before it starts the worker again. If another goroutine restarts the worker first, it returns `ErrRunningWorker`.

104.content: A stopped worker cannot be resumed. `Resume` returns `ErrWorkerStopped`. Use `Restart`, or `Start`, which also accepts a stopped worker.

105.content: The program below stops a worker, tries to resume it, adds a job while it is stopped, then restarts it.

106.content: `Start` fails on a worker that is already running, which a worker is by default (see `WithAutoRun`). `Resume` refuses the stopped worker. The job added while it was stopped waits in the queue, and runs after `Restart`.

107.content: Pause and stop never interrupt a running job. Each running job finishes first.

108.content: Jobs that have not started stay queued and are not lost. A worker may have taken several jobs from the queue at once (see how it works). On pause or stop it finishes the job it is running and parks the rest of the batch. Parked jobs are still `Queued`, and the worker's `NumPending` counts them, but the queue's `Len()` does not. They run first, in their original order, after `Resume` or `Restart`. `Purge` closes them.

109.content: A stop also cancels the worker's `Context()`. A restart gives the worker a fresh one.

110.content: `Pause`, `Resume` and `Stop` only start the change. These block until it is done:

113.content: `WaitUntilPaused` and `WaitUntilStopped` wait for one state, and never return if the worker does not reach it.

114.content: `WaitUntilIdle` waits for `Idle` with no pending jobs, so on a paused or stopped worker it keeps waiting until `Resume`, `Restart` or `Start` brings it back to `Idle` and it drains.

115.content: `WaitAndPause` and `WaitAndStop` go the other way: they call `Wait` first, then pause or stop. Waiting compares all of them.

116.content: `WithAutoRun` decides whether the worker starts when you create it. The default is `true`: `NewWorker` returns a worker that is already `Idle`, and `Start` on it returns `ErrRunningWorker`.

117.content: Pass `WithAutoRun(false)` to get an `Initiated` worker instead. You can bind queues and add jobs to it right away. The jobs wait until you call `Start`. Use it when you want to finish setting things up before any job runs.

118.content: This setting matters only for a worker with a name (`WithName` or a string argument to `NewWorker`). `Start` adds a named worker to `WorkerRegistry`, the map that the REST `Handler` reads. A worker without a name is never registered.

119.content: When a registered worker reaches `Stopped`, it stays in the registry for a while, so it still shows up as `Stopped`. `WithStoppedRetention` sets how long. When the time is up and the worker is still stopped, it is removed from the registry.

120.content: The default is one minute. `DefaultStoppedRetention` changes the default for workers created after the call.

121.content: `0` turns the cleanup off: a stopped worker stays in the registry for good.

122.content: Starting the worker again cancels the timer, and re-registers the worker if it had already been removed.

127.content: A queue belongs to one worker

128.content: A worker runs jobs; a queue holds them until the worker has a free slot. Apart from a producer-only distributed queue (`NewDistributedQueue`), you ask a worker for a queue, and that binds the two.

129.content: `BindQueue` creates an in-memory, first-in first-out queue, binds it to the worker and returns a `Queue[T]` handle. You add jobs through the handle; the worker takes them from there.

130.content: `BindQueue` is one of several ways to bind a source to a worker (`IWorkerBinder` lists them all):

137.content: A worker can have any number of queues bound to it. They all feed the same pool, so the concurrency limit covers all of them together: with concurrency 2, at most two jobs run at once, whichever queues they came from. Press Play below to watch two queues share a worker with concurrency 2, then switch to `RoundRobin` or bind a third queue.

139.content: The worker has concurrency 2 and two queues: `emails`, bound first, and `reports`. Three jobs go into each. The output shows six `Processing` lines, at most two at a time, then `All jobs done` once `WaitUntilIdle` returns. Two jobs that start together race to print, so a pair can come out in either order, `email 1` before `email 0` for example.

140.content: When a slot frees up, the worker's strategy picks which queue the next job comes from. The default strategy, `Priority`, takes the queue with the lowest priority number. Queues bound without `WithQueuePriority` tie, and a tie goes to the queue bound first, which is why every email starts before any report. `WithStrategy` switches to `RoundRobin`, `MaxLen` or `MinLen`.

141.content: With more than one queue bound, the worker hands out jobs one at a time, so the strategy decides every single job. A worker with a single in-memory queue may hand a goroutine several waiting jobs at once.

142.content: Each queue is bound to the worker that created it, and `Worker()` on the handle returns that worker. Adding a job to a queue wakes only its own worker, and each job is processed once.

143.content: To get jobs to more than one worker, use a different source:

144.content: **Every worker gets every job:** publish to a `Topic` and subscribe each worker with `WithTopic`. Topics are in-memory only.

145.content: **Workers in several processes share the jobs:** bind each one to the same distributed queue with `WithDistributedQueue`. Each job goes to one of them.

147.content: AddAll queues a slice of items in one call and returns one handle for the whole group. Wait for it, count what is pending, and read results or errors as they finish.

152.content: If you do not read the channel

153.content: `AddAll` queues a slice of `Item` values in one call. It returns one handle for the whole group, not one per job. It is a method of the in-memory queues: persistent and distributed queues have only `Add`.

155.content:
| Field  | Meaning                       |
| ------ | ----------------------------- |
| `Data` | What you would pass to `Add`. |

156.content:
| Field | Meaning                                                                           |
| ----- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ID`  | An optional job ID. The worker sees it with a `g:` prefix. Job IDs has the rules. |

157.content:
| Field      | Meaning                                                                                          |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Priority` | Read by a priority queue only. A FIFO queue ignores it. A lower number runs first, as in queues. |

158.content: The handle's type follows the worker, as it does for `Add`. Worker types compares the three.

159.content:
| Worker      | `AddAll` returns   | What you read          |
| ----------- | ------------------ | ---------------------- |
| `NewWorker` | `EnqueuedGroupJob` | nothing, you only wait |

162.content: All three have `NumPending()` and `Wait()`. The error and result handles also have `Drain()`.

163.content: `NumPending` is the number of jobs in the group that have not ended. A job ends when it runs, or when it is closed without running, by `Purge` for example. The number counts down to 0.

164.content: `Wait` blocks until `NumPending` is 0. On a plain worker, `group.Wait()` is all you need.

165.content: There is no `Close` on a group handle, and no status for a single item. To close one job, add it with `Add` instead, which gives you a handle of its own.

166.content: The scene shows the same items added both ways. Add the items, then start the worker.

167.content: `AddAll` adds the items one at a time, and skips each one the queue does not take: the queue is full or closed, or the item's ID belongs to a job still in the queue. That includes a repeated ID inside the same slice, while the first copy is still in the queue (a running worker may already have taken it). A skipped item never runs and sends nothing to `Results()` or `Errs()`. It does not count in `NumPending`, so `NumPending` can start below `len(items)`.

168.content: `AddAll` does not say which items it skipped. If you need to know, call `Add` for each job: it returns a `bool` per job.

169.content: The worker below is created with `WithAutoRun(false)`, so you can look at the group before any job runs. The third item repeats the ID `a`.

170.content: `pending: 2 of 3` shows the repeat was skipped. After `Start`, only `g:a` and `g:b` run, `Wait` returns, and `NumPending` is 0.

171.content: `Results()` returns a channel of `Result[R]` values. It returns at once. Ranging over the channel is what waits.

172.content: The worker has concurrency 3, so the three result lines can come in a different order on each run. `g:b` fails to parse and arrives as an `Err`. `pending: 0` prints after the loop ends by itself.

173.content: A `Result` has a `JobId`, a `Data` value and an `Err`. A job that succeeded has `Data`. One that failed has `Err`, and `Data` is the zero value. A panic arrives as an `Err`.

174.content: `JobId` is the item's ID with the `g:` prefix. It is empty for an item with no ID, unless the worker has a job ID generator.

175.content: Results arrive in the order the jobs finish. With concurrency above 1 that is not the order of your slice, so match results to items by `JobId`. With concurrency 1 on a FIFO queue they come back in the order you added them.

176.content: A job closed before it ran sends nothing.

177.content: The channel closes once every job in the group has ended, so the `range` loop finishes by itself.

178.content: The channel has room for one value per item. A slow reader does not hold up the workers.

179.content: `Errs()` returns a channel of `error`. It carries failures only: a job that succeeded sends nothing, so the number of values you receive is the number of jobs that failed. A panic counts as a failure. The channel closes once every job has ended, so ranging over it finishes by itself.

180.content: An error does not say which job it came from. If you need that, put the job's ID in the message, as the worker function below does with `j.ID()`.

181.content: Two of the four items are negative, so the loop receives two errors, `g:q` and `g:s`. The jobs that succeeded sent nothing.

182.content: `Drain()` discards the results or errors the channel still holds, for a caller that is not going to read them.

183.content: Do not range over `Results()` or `Errs()` after calling `AddAll` with an empty slice. With no items, no job ever ends, so nothing closes the channel and the loop never finishes. `Wait()` returns at once in that case. Check `len(items) > 0` before you read.

185.content: Set how many jobs a worker runs at once, change the limit while it runs with TunePool, and tune how many idle goroutines its pool keeps.

187.content: A limit, not a pool size

192.content: A worker's concurrency is the most jobs it runs at the same time. This page covers how to set it, how to change it while the worker runs, and the options that decide how many idle goroutines the worker keeps. How it works shows the pool behind it.

193.content: The default is 1. A plain `int` after the worker function sets it, `WithConcurrency` sets it as an option, and `DefaultConcurrency` changes the default for workers created after the call:

194.content: If you pass more than one value to a worker, the last one wins. Worker types lists the other arguments that `NewWorker` takes.

195.content: **A value below 1 means one per logical CPU.** `0` and `-1` both become `runtime.NumCPU()`, so the number depends on the machine. The same rule applies to `DefaultConcurrency` and to `TunePool`, below.

196.content: `NumConcurrency()` returns the limit. It is an upper bound on the jobs running at once, not a number of goroutines the worker creates. The worker starts a goroutine when jobs are waiting and one more would clear the backlog faster than it costs to start it, up to the limit, and goroutines exit when the backlog is gone. A worker with a limit of 100 and three waiting jobs does not start 100 goroutines. How it works has the details.

197.content: Four methods on `Worker` report what the pool is doing:

199.content:
| Method          | Returns                                                |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `NumProcessing` | the jobs running right now, counted as busy goroutines |

200.content:
| Method       | Returns                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `NumPending` | the jobs that have not started: waiting in a queue, in a batch a goroutine took, or parked by a pause or stop. While a batch runs it can read high: see waiting |

201.content:
| Method           | Returns                                           |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `NumIdleWorkers` | the idle goroutines waiting in the pool for a job |

202.content: `NumProcessing` stays at or below the limit, except for a while after `TunePool` lowers the limit. All four are snapshots: they can change right after you read them.

203.content: The program below creates a worker with a limit of 100 and holds every job inside the worker function until the program lets go. It adds three jobs, one at a time, and waits for each to start before it adds the next.

204.content: Before any job, the pool has one idle goroutine. With three jobs running, `NumProcessing` is 3, not 100. The idle goroutine took a job, so `NumIdleWorkers` is 0, and nothing is pending.

205.content: Move the limit in the scene below and watch the goroutines. The slider calls `TunePool` on a worker that keeps running: the jobs it already holds are not interrupted.

206.content: `TunePool` changes the limit of an active worker, one that is `Idle` or `Running`. It returns at once, and the new limit applies to the next job the worker hands out. A value below 1 means one per CPU, as above.

207.content: It returns an error in two cases:

208.content: `ErrSameConcurrency`: the worker already has that limit.

209.content: The worker is not `Idle` or `Running`. `TunePool` only works on an active worker, so it returns the error for the worker's state: `ErrNotRunningWorker` before `Start`, `ErrWorkerPausing` or `ErrWorkerPaused` while pausing or paused, and `ErrWorkerStopping` or `ErrWorkerStopped` while stopping or stopped. The lifecycle page has the states.

210.content: The worker starts jobs on new goroutines as soon as it can. That covers the jobs still in a queue and the jobs you add later.

211.content: A job a goroutine has already taken into a batch stays with that goroutine, which runs its batch one job after another. This matters most at concurrency 1, where one goroutine can take up to 32 jobs at once from an in-memory FIFO queue: raising the limit does not spread out jobs it already holds. How it works explains batches.

212.content: The program below starts a worker with a limit of 1 and holds every job until the program lets go. With job 1 running, it raises the limit to 3, then adds jobs 2 to 6. It adds them after the change for the reason above.

213.content: Jobs 2 and 3 start beside job 1, which is three at once, the new limit. Jobs 4 to 6 wait. The second `TunePool(3)` returns `ErrSameConcurrency`, because the worker already has a limit of 3.

214.content: Nothing running is interrupted. The worker hands out no new batch until fewer goroutines are busy than the new limit, so `NumProcessing` can stay above `NumConcurrency` until those goroutines finish their batches. A goroutine that already holds a batch keeps running it one job after another, so jobs from batches already handed out still start after the change. The worker removes idle goroutines it no longer needs at once, unless you set an expiry duration, in which case the expiry removes them (see below).

215.content: A worker with default settings keeps one idle goroutine in its pool. A goroutine that finishes a job stays in the pool if more jobs are waiting than idle goroutines are ready to run them, or if the pool holds fewer idle goroutines than the minimum, which is one. Otherwise it exits. Two options change this.

216.content: `WithMinIdleWorkerRatio` sets the share of the limit to keep idle, as a percentage from 1 to 100. The worker keeps `limit * percentage / 100` idle goroutines, rounded down, with a floor of one. With a limit of 4, a ratio of 50 keeps 2 and a ratio of 100 keeps 4. A value outside the range is clamped: `0` becomes 1 and anything above 100 becomes 100. The limit here is the current one, so the minimum follows a `TunePool`.

217.content: `WithIdleWorkerExpiryDuration` makes the pool shrink on a timer instead. With it set, a goroutine that finishes a job goes back to the pool instead of exiting. Once per duration the worker removes the goroutines that have been idle for longer than the duration, down to the minimum above. Because the check runs once per duration, a goroutine can sit idle for up to about twice the duration before it goes. Without the option there is no timer, and the pool shrinks as goroutines finish.

258.content: **Not setting the idle ratio is not the same as setting it to 1.** Without it, the worker keeps one idle goroutine. `WithMinIdleWorkerRatio(1)` keeps 1% of the limit, rounded down, and never fewer than one, so with a limit of 200 it keeps two.

259.content: **`WithName` and a string argument do the same thing.** See below.

260.content: **A queue option reaches only a queue that can use it.** `WithQueueCapacity` takes effect only on a queue that implements `CapacitySetter`, which the built-in queues do. See queues.

261.content: `NewWorker`, `NewErrWorker` and `NewResultWorker` take `config ...any` after the worker function. They read each argument by its type:

| a `ConfigFunc`, such as the value `WithAutoRun(false)` returns | applies that option |

266.content: Only a value of type `int` sets the concurrency. A value of another integer type, such as `int64` or `uint`, falls into the last row and is ignored.

267.content: The arguments are applied from left to right on top of the defaults, so the last one that sets a value wins. `varmq.NewWorker(f, 2, varmq.WithConcurrency(8))` runs 8 at once. A string and `WithName` set the same name, so with both, the later one decides. Worker types lists the same arguments next to the three constructors.

268.content: A value below 1 for the concurrency means one per CPU wherever it is given: as an `int`, in `WithConcurrency`, in `DefaultConcurrency` and in `TunePool`. The number is the logical CPU count of the machine, so it differs between machines.

269.content: Each `Default*` function sets the default of one worker option. A worker copies the defaults when you create it, so a call changes the workers created after it and leaves the ones that exist alone. An option or a positional argument for a worker still overrides the default.

270.content: **They write a package-level value with no locking.** Call them once at start-up, before any goroutine creates a worker. Calling one while another goroutine creates a worker is a data race.

271.content: **`DefaultJobIdGenerator(nil)` and `DefaultErrHandler(nil)` do nothing,** like their `With` twins. The other `Default*` functions have no such check. `DefaultCtx(nil)` goes back to no context.

280.content: Shutting down on a signal or a deadline

281.content: A worker can follow a `context.Context`. When that context is done, the worker shuts down. This page covers how to give a worker one, what the shutdown does to running and waiting jobs, and the worker's own `Context()`.

282.content: `WithContext` sets the context of one worker. `DefaultCtx` sets the context for every worker you create after the call.

283.content: Without either, the worker follows no context of yours: it behaves as if you had passed `context.Background()`, and only `Stop` and `Restart` cancel its own `Context()`. A `nil` context is the same as none.

284.content: `DefaultCtx` is shared: every worker created after it follows that one context, so cancelling it stops all of them. Configuration says when the `Default*` functions take effect.

285.content: The context does not reach your worker function. A `Job[T]` has only `Data()` and `ID()`. A function that needs the context captures it. See stopping a running job early.

286.content: When the context is done, because you called its cancel function or its deadline passed, the worker shuts down the way `Stop` does. The lifecycle page has the states. For jobs, that means:

287.content: **A running job is not interrupted.** varmq cannot stop a function. Each running job keeps going until its function returns.

288.content: **Jobs that are still waiting do not start.** Once the worker has noticed the cancel, it hands out no new job, and a goroutine that holds a batch finishes the job it is on and parks the rest. Between the cancel and the moment the worker notices, it may still hand out a job. A waiting job is not lost, and it is not closed. It stays `Queued`, either in the queue or, if a goroutine had taken it into a batch, parked on the worker. The worker's `NumPending` counts it. See what happens to jobs.

289.content: **The worker is `Stopping` while jobs run, then `Stopped`.** It reaches `Stopped` once the running jobs have returned and its goroutines are gone.

290.content: **Nothing is reported as an error.** The cancellation does not reach `Errs()` or the error handler.

291.content: **The queue keeps taking jobs.** `Add` still returns `true` after the worker has stopped, and the job waits for a worker that will not run it. `Close` on the queue makes `Add` refuse jobs, and `Purge` closes the waiting ones. See queues.

292.content: The program below adds job 1 to a worker with concurrency 1, then adds jobs 2 and 3 while job 1 runs, and cancels the context.

293.content: Right after the cancel, the worker is `Stopping` and job 1 is still running. It finishes, and the worker is `Stopped`. Jobs 2 and 3 never started. They are still in the queue, so `NumPending` and the queue's `Len()` agree. The queue still accepts job 4, which nothing will run.

294.content: Jobs 2 and 3 were still in the queue because the program added them after job 1 had started, so the worker held no batch. Had they been added first, the worker could have taken them into a batch with job 1. Jobs in a batch show in `NumPending` and not in `Len()`. See batched dispatch.

295.content: Cancelling is not the same as calling `Stop` in two ways. `Stop` sets the status to `Stopping` before it returns. A cancel function returns at once, and the worker changes its status on its own goroutine a moment later, so a status read right after it can still show the old one. And `Stop` can be undone with `Restart`, while a cancelled context cannot: see starting again after a cancel.

296.content: To wait for the shutdown, use `WaitUntilStopped`. `Wait` returns as soon as no job is running, which can be while the status is still `Stopping`. `WaitUntilIdle` keeps waiting on a stopped worker. Waiting compares them.

297.content: Because varmq does not interrupt a function, a job that should end when the worker shuts down has to watch for it. The worker's `Context()` is the one to watch: it is done when your context is, and also when `Stop` or `Restart` is called. Pass it to anything that accepts a context, or select on its `Done` channel.

298.content: The job would sleep for a second, but it ends early, as soon as the program cancels the context. `Err()` reports `context canceled`. The worker function reads `Context()` from the worker it belongs to, so the worker is declared first, as an `IWorkerBinder`.

299.content: To varmq, a job that returns early is a finished job. For a plain worker, a normal return counts as successful. With `NewErrWorker`, return the context's error if you want it counted as failed. Metrics has the counters.

300.content: `Context()` returns the worker's own context. It is a child of the one you passed with `WithContext` or `DefaultCtx`, or of `context.Background()` if you passed none. It is done when:

301.content: the context you passed is done;

304.content: Its `Err()` says why, so a deadline that passed shows as `context.DeadlineExceeded` and a cancel as `context.Canceled`. A job that waits on `Context().Done()` ends the same way when `Stop` is called.

305.content: `Restart` gives the worker a fresh `Context()`. A `Context()` you read earlier stays done. Call the method again after a restart instead of keeping the old value.

306.content: A context that is done stays done. `Start` and `Restart` give a stopped worker a new internal context, but they derive it from the context you passed, which is already done. The new one is done from the start.

307.content: Both calls still return `nil`, and the worker shuts down again at once. Before it does, it may hand out some of the jobs waiting in the queue, and they run with `Context()` already cancelled. So a cancelled context ends the worker for good. To run again, create a new worker with a context that is still live. The jobs left in the old queue stay there until you `Purge` them.

308.content: A `Stop` has no such problem: `Restart` after a `Stop` brings the worker back, because the context you passed is still live.

309.content: A context from `signal.NotifyContext` shuts the worker down on Ctrl+C. A context from `context.WithTimeout` does it when the time is up. In both cases, wait for the running jobs with `WaitUntilStopped`:

310.content: The `context-worker` example in the repository shows a worker with concurrency 10 and three-second jobs that stops on Ctrl+C. The jobs that are running finish, and the ones still waiting do not start.

318.content: Sent to Errs and the handler

319.content: A failure in varmq shows up in one of three places, and a few values are returned directly from calls you make. This page covers where a failed job is reported, how to read the worker's error channel and set an error handler, and every exported `Err` value with the call that returns it.

320.content: `Add` has no error result. It returns a `bool`, and `false` means the queue did not take the job. See queues.

321.content:
| Where                                   | What it gets                             | Which workers                        |
| --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| The job's handle: `Err()` or `Result()` | what the function returned, or the panic | `NewErrWorker` and `NewResultWorker` |

322.content:
| Where                         | What it gets                  | Which workers |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------- |
| The worker's `Errs()` channel | every failure the worker sees | all three     |

323.content:
| Where                                        | What it gets                  | Which workers |
| -------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------- |
| The error handler, set with `WithErrHandler` | every failure the worker sees | all three     |

324.content: A job's function can fail in two ways, and both are reported the same way:

325.content: **It returns an error.** An error worker or result worker sends that error to the job's handle, to `Errs()` and to the handler. The error is the same value you returned, so `errors.Is` works on it. A plain `NewWorker` function returns nothing, so it cannot fail this way.

326.content: **It panics.** The worker recovers the panic and counts the job as failed. The panic becomes an error, which goes where a returned error goes. A plain worker has no handle to carry it, so it goes to `Errs()` and the handler only.

327.content: The error for a panic reads `panic recovered inside worker: <value>`. For an error worker it is `err-worker` instead of `worker`, and for a result worker `result-worker`. The value is formatted into the text with `%v`, so `errors.Is` cannot find the panic value inside it. Worker types shows the three handles side by side.

328.content: The worker itself can also report an error that belongs to no job function: a storage problem or a failed acknowledgement. Those go to `Errs()` and the handler only.

329.content: For a group of jobs added with `AddAll`, an error group handle has its own `Errs()`. That one is a different channel, and it is closed once the group has ended. The worker's `Errs()` below is not. See adding many jobs. A failure in a group job also reaches the worker's `Errs()` and the handler.

330.content: The worker's `Errs()` returns a read-only channel of `error`. Three things to know about it:

331.content: **It holds one error.** The channel has room for a single value. When a job fails and the channel is full, the error is not put on the channel, and the worker does not wait for you. A reader that is slow, or absent, loses errors. The handler does not.

332.content: **It is never closed.** `for err := range worker.Errs()` does not end when the worker stops, so run it in a goroutine of its own, or read with `select` and a `default`.

333.content: **An error does not say which job it came from.** Put the job's ID or something that identifies the work in the message you return.

334.content: A reader like this one drains the channel as errors arrive. If you need every error, set a handler as well: the channel can still drop an error when two arrive faster than the reader takes them.

335.content: In the program below every job fails and nothing reads `Errs()` while the jobs run.

336.content: Three jobs failed, but one error waits on the channel: `job 1 failed`, the first. The other two found the channel full and were dropped, so the `select` takes its `default`. The message names the job because the program put the number in it.

337.content: `WithErrHandler` sets a function that the worker calls for every error it reports. The function receives the `Worker` and the error, so one handler can serve several workers and log the worker's `Name()`. The program below names its error worker `mailer` with a string after the function and sets a handler. Job 2 returns an error and job 3 panics.

338.content: The handler runs once for each failure and prints `mailer`. Its lines come first, because the program waits for the worker to go idle before it reads the handles. Each handle then has its own outcome: `nil`, the returned error, and the panic as `panic recovered inside err-worker: boom`.

339.content: **The handler runs for every error,** including those the full `Errs()` channel dropped.

340.content: **It runs synchronously on the goroutine that reports the error,** and it must not block. For an error from a job, or from a failed acknowledgement, that is the goroutine that ran the job, so a slow handler delays that goroutine's next job. For an error from pulling a job off its storage, it is the worker's event loop, which hands out every job, so a slow handler holds them all back.

341.content: **Passing `nil` is ignored.** The worker keeps the handler it had.

342.content: **The default handler does nothing.** `DefaultErrHandler` changes it for the workers you create after the call. Configuration says how the defaults work.

385.content: **Closures run later.** A function runs on a worker goroutine, not on the goroutine that called `Add`. Anything it captures has to be safe to share. Changing a captured variable after `Add` is a data race unless you synchronise the access.

386.content: **No persistence.** A persistent or distributed queue stores each job as JSON, and a function cannot be encoded as JSON. Keep function jobs for in-memory queues. For jobs that must survive a restart, use plain data and put the logic in the worker function.

387.content: **Naming jobs.** The job's `Data()` is the function, so nothing about the job says what it does. `WithJobId` gives it a name. See job IDs.

389.content: Give a job an ID with WithJobId, Item.ID or a generator, and use IDs to keep at most one job per ID in an in-memory queue.

396.content: A job has no ID unless you give it one: `ID()` returns an empty string. An ID names the job for your own bookkeeping. On an in-memory queue it also keeps a second job with the same ID from waiting in the queue next to the first. Jobs introduces IDs. This page has the details.

| How                  | Where                       | The job gets                         |
| -------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `WithJobId("job-1")` | an option you pass to `Add` | that ID. An empty string is ignored. |

401.content: The generator is a `func() string`. Passing `nil` is ignored. Without a generator, a job with no ID of its own has none. `DefaultJobIdGenerator` sets a generator for the workers you create after the call.

403.content: An ID from `WithJobId` or `Item.ID` takes the place of the generated one. `Add` still calls the generator when you pass `WithJobId`, and throws its value away, so a counting generator skips a number. `AddAll` calls it only for items that have no ID.

404.content: A generated ID on an `AddAll` item gets the `g:` prefix too.

405.content: `Add` calls the generator on the goroutine that calls `Add`. If several goroutines add jobs, the generator has to be safe for concurrent use.
